idiom_name: context object + context factory + request-scope binding
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define a context type that holds the per-request attributes behind typed accessors, and create and populate it once per request through a factory (optionally recycling instances from a pool to keep allocation off the request path). Then either pass it explicitly down the flow or bind it to a request scope the runtime provides (thread-local, async-local, coroutine/fiber context, request-scoped DI scope) so downstream code reads it without a parameter. Keep protocol-specific types behind the accessors, state which layer owns and may write each attribute, and guarantee that the binding is destroyed when the request ends. The explicit form remains justified when layers must stay framework-independent, when explicit dependency diagrams matter, or when the ambient runtime binding is not available (e.g. bare metal goroutines without context propagation). Modern enhancements: prefer immutable or write-once contexts to eliminate race conditions in async code; use typed keys (struct tags, enums, unexported types) rather than strings for collision-free, compile-time-checked lookups; in structured-concurrency runtimes prefer ScopedValue or ContextVar whose bindings are lexically scoped and automatically vacated when control leaves the block.
code_sketch:
ctx = ContextFactory.create(request)        # protocol values -> application values
ctx.user = authenticate(request); ctx.locale = negotiate(request)
scope.bind(ctx)                            # or dispatch(ctx) layer by layer
    layer.process()                        # reads ctx.user / ctx.locale, no parameter
scope.reset()                              # bounded lifetime: the request is over
pitfalls: Binding the context to a pooled thread or an async scope without resetting it at the end of the request leaks one request's data into the next.
Letting the context grow into an untyped bag of unrelated globals turns it into a service locator and hides the real dependencies of every component that reads it.
Storing mutable references to objects with their own lifetimes (open connections, file handles, running timers) in the context causes dangling references when the request ends.
Reading from an uninitialized or incorrectly propagated context in async child tasks (detached from the parent task tree) silently returns default values, producing wrong behaviour with no error.
Conflating the context object with a CancellationToken - components that write the context may not realise they are also potentially cancelling downstream work when they replace the token field.

Wrong move: inject the ambient holder (IHttpContextAccessor, Current, a thread-local manager) into domain services and repositories; failure: every layer regains hidden coupling to HTTP infrastructure and unit tests must stage invisible state; instead: read the context at the boundary and pass only the typed values each component declares it needs.

Wrong move: treat the context as a grab bag for collaborators and config, not per-request data; failure: it becomes a service locator, wiring disappears from constructors and nobody can tell what a component actually requires; instead: keep services in the DI container and reserve the context for request-scoped values.

Wrong move: hand the context object itself to detached background work or a long-running task; failure: the job reads another request's tenant or a recycled carrier's stale values; instead: copy the specific values (trace id, tenant, user) before spawning, or rebind a fresh context in the worker.
